targets.title: Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood
targets.thesis: God satisfies divine simplicity by being a part of all his parts, so the doctrine is best formulated as a symmetry-of-parthood thesis about God's relation to his attributes, which avoids the distinctness and modal collapse objections.

targets.title: Simple is as simple does: Plantinga and Ghazālī on divine simplicity
targets.thesis: Most of the arguments against divine simplicity credited to Plantinga were nearly perfectly anticipated by al-Ghazālī, and his responses to Avicenna's stronger form of simplicity contain new arguments that remain valuable today.

targets.title: Plantinga and Ash‘arites on Divine Simplicity
targets.thesis: The objection that no distinction can be drawn within God, so that divine attributes cannot be distinguished from God's essence, is inconsistent with the doctrine of divine simplicity, and the reductio arguments against simplicity (Plantinga, Baghdādī, Taftāzānī) rest on a mistaken presumption of such a distinction.

targets.title: Divine Simplicity and the Theory of Action
targets.thesis: God's willing to create and God's knowing creatures can be at least partly extrinsic (Cambridge) properties, because a general theory of action allows an agent to remain intrinsically unchanged across different effects, and free volition is such a causal relation.
